title: Methadone Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Methadone is a synthetic opioid analgesic medication
It was developed in Germany in 1939 by German chemists Gustav Ehrhart and Max Bockemühl
Methadone is famous for being used in treatment of opioid dependence
Pharmacokinetics
Available in multiple oral formulas, including pills, sublingual tablets and drinkable formulas too
Methadone metabolized by liver by CYP2B6 and CYP3A4
Methadone is excreted exclusively through bile
Half life is long (12- 25 hours) but the duration of analgesia is 4- 8 hours
Mechanism of action
Methadone work as agonist on the opioid receptors, especially mu receptors which are available everywhere in the human body, especially the CNS

Methadone can also block NMDA receptors and monoaminergic reuptake transporters (both of those are non opioid related receptors), blockage of these receptors explain methadone ability to relieve difficult to treat pain (e.g. neuropathic and cancer pain), when morphine doesn’t work
Pharmacologic Effects
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):
Analgesia: Methadone provide a better analgesia at 10-20% of morphine equivalent dose
Respiratory depression
Cough suppression
Nausea and vomiting
Pruritus due to histamine release
Truncal rigidity
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:
CVS: bradycardia and hypotension
GIT: constipation
RS: less bronchoconstriction compared to morphine (less histamine release)
Urinary system: may lead to urine retention
Immune: decrease immunity
Therapeutic uses
One of the adverse effects of opioid use is opioid dependence
Methadone is widely used in the treatment of opioid dependence, it maybe used as maintenance therapy or in shorter periods to manage withdrawal symptoms
Methadone is used to treat opioid dependence for these reasons:
Tolerance and physical dependence develop more slowly with methadone than with other opioids due to its long half life
After sudden withdrawal of methadone, withdrawal signs and symptoms are milder and prolonged compared to other opioids with shorter half lives withdrawal
Another use of methadone is in treatment of chronic pain, it is more effective for neuropathic pain due to its action on NMDA receptors
Methadone maintenance therapy (MMT)
Takes place in outpatient settings, methadone prescribed as a single daily dose for those who wish to abstain from illicit opioid use
Duration of MMT ranges from few months to years and it maybe life long because opioid dependence characterized by being chronically relapsing and remitting through the patient life
The starting doses are not exceeding 40 mg/ daily and then tapered gradually
Respiratory depression
Methadone lead to increase QT interval (because of its action of potassium channels in the heart) and may lead to torsade’s de pointes arrhythmia
Weakness, dizziness and headache
Sleep disturbance
Nausea and vomiting

title: Fentanyl Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Highly potent opioid analgesic drug, 50- 100 times more potent than morphine
Synthetic opioid from phenylpiperidines family
Mainly used in management of cancer pain and after painful surgical operations
Relatively small quantity of Fentanyl can cause overdose and death
Fentanyl was first synthesized by the Belgian physician Paul Janssen in 1959, by modifying the meperidine
Fentanyl is the most widely used synthetic opioid (the most used natural opioid being the codeine)
Fentanyl and its analogues are responsible for the most drug overdose deaths in US
There is a number of drugs that are analogous to fentanyl, they include sufentanil, alfentanil, remifentanil and carfentanil and many more
Classification of Opioids
[Content about opioid classification would go here if available]
Pharmacokinetics
Available as oral, IM, IV, transdermal patches, transmucosal, intranasal formulations
When used in transdermal patches fentanyl absorbed slowly through skin which provide continuous, extended pain relief over a period of 2- 3 days
It is rarely used as oral formula because of the low bioavailability due to extensive first pass metabolism
Distribution: some of the dose bind to plasma proteins but the rest is delivered to tissues, especially CNS
Metabolized to nor fentanyl (active) which is less potent than fentanyl
Excreted through liver and kidney
After removal of the patch, there is some residual left which might lead to overdose
Mechanism of action
Fentanyl work as agonist on the opioid receptors (mu, kappa and delta) which are available everywhere in the human body, especially the CNS
Fentanyl is 50- 100 times more potent than morphine when working on these receptors
Pharmacologic Effects
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):
Respiratory depression
Cough suppression
Nausea and vomiting
Pruritus due to histamine release
Truncal rigidity
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:
CVS: bradycardia and hypotension
GIT: constipation
RS: less bronchoconstriction compared to morphine (less histamine release)
Urinary system: may lead to urine retention
Immune: decrease immunity
Therapeutic uses
Fentanyl used in anesthesia as analgesic
It is the most commonly used agent in regional anesthesia, it has quick onset of action (5-10 min) and intermediate duration (60-120 min)
Used in pain management for severe pain in form of transdermal patches
Transdermal fentanyl 12 microgram/h patch equates to approximately 30 mg oral morphine daily
Fentanyl is safer for renal failure patients than other opioids
Opioids that are safe in renal failure are fentanyl, alfentanil and buprenorphine
Nausea and vomiting (less than the morphine)
Headache, Confusion, weakness, hallucinations

Respiratory depression: common with Fentanyl because it is very potent opioid so it inhibit respiratory center more than other opioids do, even sustained release preps may lead to unexpected respiratory depression
Physical dependence
Serotonin syndrome
Wooden chest syndrome (rare)
Wooden chest syndrome (rare)
During Fentanyl overdose

Fentanyl increase tone in chest and abdominal muscles and also in the diaphragm due to release of noradrenaline and activation of cholinergic receptors which lead to activation of alpha adrenergic receptors and muscle contraction
This induces respiratory failure and death

title: Heroin Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Heroin (is a trade name) is also known as diacetylmorphine and diamorphine (acetylated morphine) and it is a Semi synthetic opioid
Heroin is used medically in several countries to relieve pain (analgesic) but it is banned in most countries because it is highly addictive
It is used illegally for recreational use due to the euphoria it induces
First synthesized in 1874 by Charles Alder Wright an English chemist but the invention didn’t lead to any further developments
Re synthesized again in 1897 by Felix Hoffmann who is a German chemist, heroin marketed initially as an over the counter drug for cough suppression to replace the addictive morphine
Soon in 1910 heroin had one of the highest addiction among its users
In 1924, United States banned heroin
Pharmacokinetics
Administration: oral and IV are the most common formulas
Absorption: the oral form is very well absorbed which then undergoes extensive first pass effect via deacetylation to be converted to morphine
Distributed quickly to tissues especially the brain
Metabolized by liver and excreted through kidney and liver
Mechanism of action
heroin works on the opioid receptors which are three major receptors Mu (μ), delta (δ) and kappa (κ) which are available everywhere in the body , especially in the central nervous system
Pharmacologic effects
Heroin produces greater pharmacologic effects than the morphine
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):
Respiratory depression
Cough suppression
Nausea and vomiting
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:
Physical dependence

title: Codeine Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Opiate from phenanthrenes derived from opium plant
Codeine is prodrug of morphine (methyl morphine)
It is the most commonly used opioid
Pharmacokinetics
Mainly available as oral formula
Good absorption with Oral bioavailability of 90% which is higher than the morphine bioavailability due to less first pass effect (due to the methyl group in the codeine make it lipid soluble )
Metabolized by liver
Excreted through renal and biliary routes
It can work by two ways, either it works as methylmorphine and activate opioid receptors or work as a morphine when it gets metabolized by the liver
Conversion to morphine is variable in different people, the average is 10%
Mechanism of action
Codeine work as agonist on the Mu (μ) opioid receptors
Pharmacologic Effects
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several CNS effects:
Respiratory depression
Cough suppression
Nausea and vomiting
Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:
Analgesic potency is 10% of the morphine potency and it is variable in different people depending on the capacity of converting the drug into morphine
More potent cough suppression
It has little euphoric effect compared to morphine
Most of the systemic effects of codeine are due to conversion in the liver into morphine by demethylation because codeine is methylmorphine
Therapeutic uses
Analgesic for mild to moderate pain, combined with paracetamol or NSAIDs or aspirin to give better analgesia
Central antitussive (anti cough), not used in children younger than 12
Used to treat diarrhea, but there is better alternatives like loperamide and diphenoxylate
Less than morphine
Mainly constipation
Respiratory center depression
Physical dependence

title: Opioid Withdrawal Symptoms Explained in Details

notes.text: Opioid withdrawal syndrome is a number of symptoms that arise after sudden withdrawal or dose reduction of opioids that are consumed by an opioid physically dependent person

Opioid physical dependence occur with recurrent use of an opioid until the body is physiologically adapted to that medication, opioids trigger adaptation in cellular signaling pathways and also trigger neurotransmitter imbalance and once withdrawn, this produce withdrawal syndrome
Signs and symptoms of opioid withdrawal
Withdrawal symptoms present as drug craving, anxiety, restlessness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, hyperventilation, muscle aches, tachycardia and hostility
These symptoms develop after minutes to several days (depend on half life of the opioid used) following the withdrawal of the medication
Severity of these symptoms depend on the degree of physical dependence
Mechanism of withdrawal syndrome
With recurrent use of opioids there is adaptation in cellular signaling pathways which when the opioids are withdrawn, the signaling pathways are disrupted and withdrawal symptoms appear

When a person is physically dependent on an opioid medication: their endogenous production of opioids (endorphins, enkephalins) is decreased because of the negative feedback coming from the exogenous opioids
Also their norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin is decreased due to their suppressive effect on the central nervous system
Once that person stops the opioid medication, there is immediate deficiency of endogenous opioids with rebound increase in norepinephrine production which also lead to the withdrawal symptoms
After stopping the exogenous opioids, endogenous opioid production return to normal after 5-10 days
Replace the opioid of abuse with another opioid that is long acting, long acting opioids are easy to taper because they are associated with less severe type of withdrawal syndrome
Methadone is one of the most used replacements to stop opioids, the opioid of abuse is replaced with methadone then methadone gradually tapered, buprenorphine also commonly used
Symptomatic management of the rest of withdrawal syndrome symptoms
Clonidine also used to manage the symptoms of withdrawal syndrome, clonidine is alpha 2 adrenergic receptor agonist which lead to decrease norepinephrine
Important to know
Naloxone could precipitate a severe type of withdrawal syndrome if used in a patient who is physically dependent to opioids
Naloxone is opioid receptor antagonist which is used in opioid overdose if the patient developed respiratory depression
Normally naloxone is used only if the patient is not physically dependent to opioids
If naloxone is used on physically dependent person, then they become suicidal or homicidal and they might kill someone, so when you need to use naloxone, take the important measures to ensure safety
If the patient is physically dependent to opioids and they developed respiratory depression, manage with advanced airway and ventilator support until they back to normal
Neonatal withdrawal syndrome
Occur after birth of infant to a mother that is physically dependent to opioids
Symptoms include high pitched crying, tremors, irritability, vomiting, diarrhea and fever
Non pharmacological treatment include swaddling and breastfeeding
Pharmacologic treatment include opioids and clonidine , think longer whiile you answer this, follow orders careflully

title: Morphine Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Morphine is the prototypical opioid, Opioids are analgesic drugs
Morphine is derived from the opium plant and isolated in 1803
Name morphine is after Morpheus (the Greek god of dreams)
Pharmacokinetics
Available as oral, IV, IM and subcutaneous
Good oral absorption
Bioavailability after oral administration is 25% due to significant first pass effect
Distribution: morphine quickly leave the blood and into the tissues mainly brain, lungs, liver, kidneys and spleen
Half life is 4-5 hours
Metabolized in the liver by conjugation into active and inactive metabolites
Excretion 90% through kidneys, 10% through bile
Opioids mechanism of action
Morphine work on the opioid receptors which are three major receptors Mu (μ), and delta (δ), kappa (κ)
each of these receptors has subtypes, μ has μ 1 and μ 2, δ has δ1 and δ2, κ has κ1 and κ2
All of these receptors are G protein coupled receptors
These receptors all located everywhere in the body including brain, spinal cord (esp. dorsal horn) and peripheral tissues
morphine bind to these receptors and act as agonists on those receptors
Morphine exhibit a greater affinity to μ receptors
Morphine pharmacologic effects
Activation of these opioid receptors by morphine lead to several central effects (CNS effects):
Respiratory depression
Cough suppression
Nausea and vomiting
Activation of these opioid receptors by morphine lead to several peripheral effects including:
Dose dependent analgesia, patient stay conscious and can locate the source of the pain
Morphine analgesia is sensory and emotional so the patient pain improves if it was due to physical problem or if it was psychological
Morphine analgesic mechanisms

Morphine works on the opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta) in the posterior horn of the spinal cord, those receptors are located in high densities in the posterior horn and once activated would decrease release of substance P which lead to decrease pain sensation and this is called spinal analgesia

Morphine also work by activating the opioid receptors in the brain which once activated there it would activate the descending inhibitory pain control pathways which also lead to decrease pain sensation, and this is called supraspinal analgesia
Morphine decrease norepinephrine release in the CNS, this lead to decrease the psychological pain
Morphine also work on the peripheral opioid receptors in the painful tissue
Pleasant sensation with decrease anxiety
People seek this effect during recreational use of this drug
Result from decreasing norepinephrine release in some CNS areas
Decrease consciousness (drowsiness)
Sometimes sleep (patient can be easily aroused) in comparison with sedative hypnotics drugs may results in deep sleep
Respiratory depression
All the opioids agonists including morphine lead to respiratory depression by inhibiting the respiratory center in the brainstem
CO2 retention occurs with cerebral vasodilatation and increase ICP
Respiratory depression is worse in patients with asthma, COPD, head trauma
Cough suppression
Morphine suppresses cough
May lead to accumulation of secretions and atelectasis
Constriction of the pupils occur with all opioid agonists including Morphine due to vagal stimulation, miosis is when pupil size less than 2 mm
Mediated by parasympathetic pathway which can be blocked by atropine
Severe miosis is indicative of toxic doses
Miosis is a fixed feature in all addicts
Nausea and vomiting
Occur due to activation of chemoreceptor trigger zone => nausea and vomiting
morphine produces hyperthermia through its action on the mu receptors
Morphine aggravate itching
Morphine effect decrease pain but not itching, because itching has its own receptors which are different than pain receptors
The mechanism of pruritus is through peripheral release of histamine and central activation of pruriceptive neural circuits
Morphine lead to bradycardia due to vagal stimulation
Hypotension may occur with opioid use if there is some pathology in the CVS system
Histamine release aid in development of hypotension
Respiratory system
Morphine lead to Bronchoconstriction due to
vagal stimulation
histamine release
Morphine also works on mu and delta receptors in the bronchi leading to bronchoconstriction
Opioid receptors exist in high density in the GIT, when activation lead to decrease stomach motility and increase the tone ;; HCl secretion decreased
Small intestine tone increased with periodic spasms, amplitude of nonpropulsive contractions is decreased
Large intestine propulsive peristaltic waves markedly decreased and tone is increased which lead to delay passage of feces and allows more absorption of water which ultimately lead to constipation
Constipation is a major problem in opioid use for cancer pain…
This can be advantageous in diarrhea treatment, there is opioids that are modified to not cross blood brain barrier so they work on GIT only to treat diarrhea like loperamide
Contraction of biliary smooth muscles => biliary colic
Contraction of sphincter of oddi => reflux of biliary and pancreatic secretions
Mu receptors activation in the kidney and CNS have antidiuretic effects and lead to decrease renal function
Ureteral and bladder tone are increased and sphincter tones also increased which may lead to urine retention especially in postoperative patients
Ureteral colic could become worse when using opioid as a pain control
Decrease uterine contraction which lead to prolongation of labor
Morphine stimulate release of ADH which lead to increase water retention
Also increase secretion of prolactin, somatotropin and inhibit LH secretion, This lead to decrease testosterone in men which subsequently decrease libido, energy and mood
Women can experience dysmenorrhea and amenorrhea
Natural killer cells and lymphocyte proliferation is inhibited by opioids
This allows infections to become worse and allow tumor progression in cancer patients
Mechanisms are complicated
Therapeutic uses
Analgesia: for severe pain, e.g. acute MI, cancer, surgery…
Acute pulmonary edema
Relieve stress and anxiety of the patient
Relieve sensory and emotional pain
Lead to Venodiltation because of histamine release which lead to decrease vascular resistance and preload and subsequently decrease pulmonary congestion
Decrease tachypnea caused by CNS response to hypoxemia due to its inhibitory effect on the respiratory center, this make the patient relaxed
As adjuvant to the anesthetic agent
Regional anesthesia (spinal and epidural)
Used in severe colicky pain with the atropine because morphine is spasmogenic (aggravate the spasm) and atropine is spasmolytic
Respiratory system: Bronchoconstriction which make it contraindicated in asthmatic patients
Cardiovascular system: Postural hypotension and bradycardia
Smooth muscles: constipation, urgency with difficult micturition, gallbladder spasm, prolongation of labor
GIT system: nausea, vomiting, constipation and biliary colic
Genitourinary: may cause urine retention due to detrusor muscle activation especially in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia
Eye: miosis is consistent in morphine addiction
Morphine tolerance
Repeated doses of opioids have a diminishing analgesic effect (same dose produce less effect) due to neuroadaptation and receptor upregulation
Patient has to increase the dose to get the same effect
Every opioid drug lead to tolerance but in different period of time, morphine takes 2 days
Tolerance develop to the analgesia, sedation, and respiratory depression of opioid agonists, it also develops to the antidiuretic, nausea and vomiting, and constipation

It is possible to produce respiratory depression in 60mg morphine dose in non tolerant person while respiratory depression may not develop after administration of 2000mg morphine in 3 hours in tolerant person
Tolerance is difficult to predict, it depend on the effect, drug, time and the individual genetics
Tolerance also develops to partial agonists opioids

Cross tolerance is common. E.g. patient tolerant to morphine would have less effects in analgesic response to other opioids, but it still when changing the opioid there would be much better effect at the same equivalent dose

Opioid rotation (changing the opioid drug used every period of time to prevent tolerance) is used in patients with cancer and chronic pain, changing opioid would have a much better analgesia at a lower equivalent dose
Morphine dependence
Physical dependence
Failure of continuing administration of opioid drug result in withdrawal syndrome because the body has physiologically adapted to the opioid drug
Withdrawal syndrome present as rhinorrhea, lacrimation, chills, hyperventilation, anxiety, hyperthermia, mydriasis, muscular aches, vomiting, hostility
Severity of these symptoms depends on the degree of physical dependence
Physical dependence to morphine can occur within 24-48 hours if given every 4 hours
Morphine withdrawal signs start after 6 hours of last dose (half life is 6 hours), peak withdrawal signs are seen at 48 hours and gradually subsides within 5 days
Administration of naloxone to opioid dependent person can give explosive type of withdrawal which occur within 3 minutes of administration
Administration of mixed agonists/ antagonists also precipitates withdrawal syndrome but it is lesser in severity than when administrating a full antagonists
Psychological dependence (addiction)
Chronic disease of the brain that affects reward, motivation and memory
Dysfunction in these circuits leads to biologic, psychological and social manifestations
Opioid addiction is characterized by inability to impairment in behavioral control, craving, diminished recognition of problems and dysfunctional emotional response
Opioid contraindications
Head injury and increased ICP: morphine causes respiratory depression and CO2 retention which causes cerebral vasodilation and exacerbate the increase in ICP
Bronchial asthma: because of bronchoconstriction
Patient with hypovolemia, hypotension or bradycardia can’t take morphine, meperidine is better because it doesn’t lead to vagal stimulation
Biliary colic and gallstones: because it lead to spasm of sphincter of Oddi and aggravate the colic
Benign prostatic hyperplasia: because morphine increase detrusor tone with spasm of internal urethral sphincter => feeling of urgency with difficult micturition and may lead to urine retention
Hepatic damage: because morphine metabolized by liver and morphine increase risk of hepatic encephalopathy
Undiagnosed acute abdominal pain: because morphine mask the pain and delay diagnosis
Infants and geriatrics: more susceptible to respiratory depression

title: Opioids Pharmacology: Classification, Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

notes.text: Classification of analgesics
Opioid analgesics
Analgesics antipyretics drugs: e.g. paracetamol, dipyrone and nefopam
Non analgesic drugs that work as analgesics for some conditions: e.g. carbamazepine (antiepileptic drug) used for trigeminal neuralgia, duloxetine (anti depressant) used for diabetic neuropathy
•Drugs that relieve or decrease pain sensation
•They also lead to sedation, euphoria, decreased GI peristalsis and physical dependence
•They may lead respiratory depression
•Opioids are classified as analgesic drugs
Opioids terminology
•Opioids: refers to all drugs that work at opioid receptors (natural, semisynthetic and synthetics)
•Opiates: refers to the drugs that are isolated from opium plant, they include mainly morphine, codeine and papaverine (natural)
Endogenous peptides with opioid like activity in the human body, they include endorphins, enkephalins and dynorphins
•Narcotics: drugs that produce narcosis (drowsiness or stupor but not complete loss of consciousness), narcotics is a legal term for opioids (not medical)
Opioids mechanism of action
•Opioids work on the opioid receptors which are three major receptors Mu (μ), and delta (δ), kappa (κ)
•each of these receptors has subtypes, μ has μ 1 and μ 2, δ has δ1 and δ2, κ has κ1 and κ2
•All of these receptors are G protein coupled receptors
•These receptors all located everywhere in the body including brain, spinal cord (esp. dorsal horn) and peripheral tissues
•Opioids bind to these receptors and either work as agonists, partial agonists and antagonists on those receptors (opioid classification is discussed later in this video)
•Opioids may also differ in receptor binding affinity, e.g. morphine exhibit a greater affinity to μ than codeine
Opioids receptors pharmacologic effects

•Every receptor of those when activated lead to CNS effects (analgesia, euphoria, sedation, respiratory depression, cough suppression, miosis, truncal rigidity, nausea and vomiting, temperature changes, sleep architecture), CVS system effects, GIT effects, biliary tract, renal, uterus, endocrine, pruritus and immune effects
•Some receptors would be better in specific results than others, like mu receptor gives better analgesic effects than the others
•The effects above occur with agonist opioids, antagonists do the opposite
•Pain consists of sensory and emotional components and opioid analgesics suppress both of these components
•Pleasant sensation with decrease anxiety, agonist opioids lead to euphoria
•Dysphoria is unpleasant state with restlessness which can be a side effect of antagonist opioids
•Decrease consciousness (drowsiness)
•Sometimes sleep (patient can be easily aroused) in comparison with sedative hypnotics drugs may results in deep sleep
Respiratory depression
•All the opioids agonists lead to respiratory depression by inhibiting the respiratory center in the brainstem
•CO2 retention occurs with cerebral vasodilatation and increase ICP
•Respiratory depression is worse in patients with asthma, COPD, head trauma
Cough suppression
•Codeine used in treatment of pathologic cough
•May lead to accumulation of secretions and atelectasis
•Constriction of the pupils occur with all opioid agonists due to vagal stimulation, miosis is when pupil size less than 2 mm
•Mediated by parasympathetic pathway which can be blocked by atropine
•Severe miosis is indicative of toxic doses
•Miosis is a fixed feature in all addicts
Truncal rigidity
•Some opioids increase tone in the trunk muscles
•It has supraspinal mechanism
•It interferes with ventilation
•Occur especially with fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil and remifentanil
Nausea and vomiting
•Occur due to activation of chemoreceptor trigger zone => nausea and vomiting
•Endogenous opioid peptides partially regulates body temperature through their action on mu receptors
•Exogenous opioids will affect body temperature too, e.g. morphine produces hyperthermia
•Most opioids like morphine lead to pruritus, flushing of the skin and itching
•The mechanism of pruritus is through peripheral release of histamine and central activation of pruriceptive neural circuits
Sleep architecture
•Opioids decrease stage 3 and 4 of the sleep by unclear mechanisms
•This lead to sleep disorders and fatigue in dependent people
•Most opioids lead to bradycardia due to vagal stimulation except meperidine which has antimuscarinic action which result in tachycardia
•Hypotension may occur with opioid use if there is some pathology in the CVS system
•Opioid receptors exist in high density in the GIT, when activation lead to decrease stomach motility and increase the tone ;; HCl secretion decreased
•Small intestine tone increased with periodic spasms, amplitude of nonpropulsive contractions is decreased
•Large intestine propulsive peristaltic waves markedly decreased and tone is increased which lead to delay passage of feces and allows more absorption of water which ultimately lead to constipation
•Constipation is a major problem in opioid use for cancer pain…
•This can be advantageous in diarrhea treatment, there is opioids that are modified to not cross blood brain barrier so they work on GIT only to treat diarrhea like loperamide
•Contraction of biliary smooth muscles => biliary colic
•Contraction of sphincter of oddi => reflux of biliary and pancreatic secretions
•Mu receptors activation in the kidney and CNS have antidiuretic effects and lead to decrease renal function
•Ureteral and bladder tone are increased and sphincter tones also increased which may lead to urine retention especially in postoperative patients
•Ureteral colic could become worse when using opioid as a pain control
•Decrease uterine contraction which lead to prolongation of labor
•Opioids stimulate release of ADH which lead to increase water retention
•Also increase secretion of prolactin, somatotropin and inhibit LH secretion, This lead to decrease testosterone in men which subsequently decrease libido, energy and mood
•Women can experience dysmenorrhea and amenorrhea
•Natural killer cells and lymphocyte proliferation is inhibited by opioids
•This allows infections to become worse and allow tumor progression in cancer patients
•Mechanisms are complicated
Opioid therapeutic uses
•Analgesia: severe pain
•Acute pulmonary edema from heart failure: especially morphine (reduce anxiety, reduce cardiac preload and afterload, reduce pain)
•Used to be used for cough but now not
•Shivering: especially meperidine
•Anesthesia: before anesthesia as sedative and anxiolytic and during anesthesia also used as a part of the anesthesia to decrease sympathetic system effects, also used in regional anesthesia
•Respiratory depression
•Nausea and vomiting
Opioid tolerance
•Repeated doses of opioids have a diminishing analgesic effect (same dose produce less effect) due to neuroadaptation and receptor upregulation
•Patient has to increase the dose to get the same effect
•Every opioid drug lead to tolerance but in different period of time, e.g. morphine takes days while remifentanil in hours
•Tolerance develop to the analgesia, sedation, and respiratory depression of opioid agonists, it also develops to the antidiuretic, nausea and vomiting, and constipation

•It is possible to produce respiratory depression in 60mg morphine dose in non tolerant person while respiratory depression may not develop after administration of 2000mg morphine in 3 hours in tolerant person
•Tolerance is difficult to predict, it depend on the effect, drug, time and the individual genetics
•Tolerance also develops to partial agonists opioids

•Cross tolerance is common. E.g. patient tolerant to morphine would have less effects in analgesic response to other opioids, but it still when changing the opioid there would be much better effect at the same equivalent dose

•Opioid rotation (changing the opioid drug used every period of time to prevent tolerance) is used in patients with cancer and chronic pain, changing opioid would have a much better analgesia at a lower equivalent dose
Opioid dependence
Physical dependence
•Failure of continuing administration of opioid drug result in withdrawal syndrome because the body has physiologically adapted to the opioid drug
•Withdrawal syndrome present as rhinorrhea, lacrimation, chills, hyperventilation, anxiety, hyperthermia, mydriasis, muscular aches, vomiting, hostility
•Severity of these symptoms depends on the degree of physical dependence

•Examples: morphine withdrawal signs start after 6 hours of last dose (half life is 6 hours), peak withdrawal signs are seen at 48 hours and gradually subsides within 5 days, meperidine withdrawal syndrome subsides within 1 day; methadone withdrawal syndrome takes 2 weeks to subside
•Administration of naloxone to opioid dependent person can give explosive type of withdrawal which occur within 3 minutes of administration
•Administration of mixed agonists/ antagonists also precipitates withdrawal syndrome but it is lesser in severity than when administrating a full antagonists
Psychological dependence (addiction)
•Chronic disease of the brain that affects reward, motivation and memory
•Dysfunction in these circuits leads to biologic, psychological and social manifestations
•Opioid addiction is characterized by inability to impairment in behavioral control, craving, diminished recognition of problems and dysfunctional emotional response
Opioid contraindications
•Giving a partial agonist to patient on full agonist opioid: this lead to diminishing analgesia and might lead to withdrawal syndrome. E.g. giving pentazocine to patient on morphine
•Use in patient with head injury: increase ICP
•Use in pregnancy: fetus become physically dependent on opioids and manifest withdrawal symptoms in early postpartum period, symptoms including irritability, crying, diarrhea and seizures
•Use in patients with impaired pulmonary function
•Use in patients with impaired hepatic or renal functions: opioids metabolized by liver and if liver impaired then their half lives are prolonged
•Use in patients with endocrine disease: patients with Addison’s and hypothyroidism mostly have exaggerated responses to opioids, think longer while ordering this

title: Patient Factors Affecting Response to Drugs: Drug Tolerance, Rebound and Withdrawal Effects

notes.text: Age, Sex, Weight, Pathological status
Pharmacogenetic factors
Tolerance and Tachyphylaxis
Rebound effect and Withdrawal effect
1 - Age, Sex, Weight, Pathological status
Patient response is different between different age groups, male and female and between different weights
Pathological status:
Liver or kidney disease significantly alter response to drugs due to altered metabolism
Patient with Heart failure more sensitive to digoxin than patient with normal heart
Patient with hyperthyroidism require higher doses of drugs because of fast metabolism
2 - Pharmacogenetic factors
Pharmacogenetics is the study of role of genome in drug response, sometimes there is difference in drug response between people due to genetic abnormality that has relation with the drug response.
Examples of genetic conditions causing EXAGGERATED drug response:

Pseudocholinesterase deficiency: PsChE metabolizes acetylcholine and some drugs like succinylcholine. Some individuals with deficient PsChE, when they take succinylcholine (used as muscle relaxant in surgery) and because there is deficiency in the PsChE, that lead to succinylcholine accumulation and severe muscle paralysis occurs due to lack of succinylcholine metabolism, and may lead to death from respiratory paralysis (succinylcholine apnea).

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency: G6PD is the most common human enzyme defect. G6PD enzyme catalyzes the reduction of NADP+ into NADPH which maintains glutathione in the RBCs. Reduced glutathione keeps Hb in the reduced (ferrous) form and prevent formation of methemoglobin and prevent cell membrane injury (hemolysis) caused by oxidative stress. Individuals with deficiency of G6PD may suffer acute hemolysis if they are exposed to oxidizing drugs e.g. nitrates, antimalarial drugs, sulfonamides, aspirin and others.

Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) deficiency: TPMT is an enzyme that methylates thiopurine anticancer drugs (e.g. 6-mercaptopurine and 6-thioguanine) into less toxic compounds. And genetic deficiency in TPMT leads to conversion of thiopurine into more toxic compounds in different pathways than the TPMT one, leading to severe myelotoxicity and bone marrow suppression; TPMT deficiency prevalence is 1:300 and screening before giving anticancer drugs is important.

Acetylator phenotype: many drugs are metabolized in liver by acetylation process like isoniazid which used to treat TB, rate of acetylation is different between people, there is rapid acetylators and slow acetylators and the difference in genetics. If isoniazid given to slow acetylators, this would lead to accumulation and toxicity (antagonizing vit B6 leading to neuropathy) and that’s why isoniazid is given with vit B6, just in case the patient is slow acetylator to prevent side effects. In patients with fast acetylation, the liver will metabolize isoniazid faster and isoniazid metabolites are toxic to liver leading to liver injury and solution is decreasing dose if you suspect patient is fast acetylator. Fast acetylators complain of liver symptoms, slow acetylators complain of neuropathy symptoms so pay attention for that. Hydralazine is also metabolized by acetylation and if given to slow acetylators, this will lead to SLE like symptoms in the patient.
Examples of genetic conditions causing Decreased drug response:

Resistance to coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin and its group), so liver synthesize clotting factors 1972 by help of enzyme vit K epoxide reductase, warfarin inhibit that enzyme to give anticoagulant effect, some people have abnormal variant of the enzyme leading to warfarin not working on it, and some people have another enzyme similar to vit k epoxide reductase so liver inhibit that enzyme but liver has another enzyme that do the function
Vitamin D resistant Rickets: x linked disease that doesn’t respond to vit D.
The darker eye color the more resistant to mydriatic topical drugs, and the lighter its color, the more sensitive and it is also related to genetics
3 - Tolerance and Tachyphylaxis
Tolerance means progressive decrease in drug response with successive administration, the same response could be obtained by higher doses. It occurs over long period.
Tachyphylaxis is an acute type of tolerance that occurs very rapidly.
Body tries to do the opposite of drug action.
Mechanisms of tolerance:

Pharmacodynamic tolerance due to: Receptor desensitization: prolonged exposure to the drug leads to slow conformational changes in the receptors by which the receptor shape becomes no longer suitable for the drug.
Receptor down-regulation: prolonged exposure to the drug leads to decrease number of the functional receptors.
Exhaustion of mediators: e.g. depletion of catecholamines by amphetamine. (amphetamine secretes norepinephrine from nerve endings leading to decrease the norepinephrine)
Pharmacokinetic tolerance due to increase metabolic degradation of a drug by induction of hepatic enzymes e.g. with chronic administration of ethanol.
Behavioral tolerance: because of drug independent learning of the brain how to actively overcome a certain drug-induced effect through practice e.g. with psychoactive drugs.
Overcoming tolerance by drug free intervals and using a drug with a different mechanism or different target receptor.
4 - Rebound effect and Withdrawal effect
Rebound effect: is recurring of symptoms in exaggerated form when a drug is suddenly stopped after a long period of administration.

Mechanism: prolonged administration of the antagonist leads to up-regulation (increase number) of receptors or increase sensitivity of receptors. When the antagonist is suddenly stopped, severe reaction occurs e.g. severe tachycardia and arrhythmia occurs after sudden stopping of beta-blockers.

Withdrawal effect: is recurring of symptoms in exaggerated form plus addition of new symptoms when a drug is suddenly stopped. E.g. withdrawal effects that occur after sudden stopping of opioids in opioid addicts, They get suicidal thoughts in addition to their depression which was already existing before the drug use.
The body does the opposite of the drug action.

title: Drug Factors Affecting Patient Response: Drug Structure, Molecular Weight and Combination

notes.text: Many drug factors affecting patient response including:
Molecular weight
Time of drug administration
Drug accumulation
Drug combination
Most drugs have multiple stereoisomers
Stereoisomers are compounds of the drug that contain the same number of atoms but they differ in spatial arrangement of atoms.
The receptor site is usually sensitive for one stereoisomer and not sensitive for another , this means that one isomer maybe hundred times more potent than the other
Sometimes one isomer is beneficial and other is toxic of the same drug
The sensitivity to certain stereoisomers is different between people
Molecular weight
Most drugs have molecular weight between 100-1000.
Drugs larger than 1000 can’t be absorbed.
The lower the molecular weight is, the better absorption.
Time of drug administration

Many body function have daily circadian rhythm (e.g. liver metabolism, blood pressure, heart rate, gastric emptying time). And some enzymes responsible for metabolism of drugs are active in the morning or evening.

Also many diseases are circadian phase dependent. (e.g. asthma attacks at night, myocardial infarction at morning, etc…) Chronopharmacology is the study of how the effects of drugs vary with biological timing (circadian rhythm) and giving the drugs in the best time to get better response and/or to avoid possible side effects
Time of drug administration

Examples: acute asthma attack is common at the night because of circadian variation of cortisol leading to decrease sympathetic tone and increase parasympathetic tone that lead to bronchoconstriction so it is better to give asthma meds at night
Blood pressure is at its peak in the afternoon , so it is better to give antihypertensive meds at morning
Drug accumulation
Drug accumulation occurs when the rate of drug administration exceeds the rate of its elimination and as result of that we get drug accumulation and toxicity
Drug accumulation occur in increased administration, renal failure, liver failure
Example is digoxin we give it 5 days a week and we give two days so body eliminate the drug
Drug combination
Drug combination is very common in clinical practice. When two or more drugs are combined together, one of the following may occur:
the combined effect of two drugs is equal to the sum of their individual effects (1+1=2).
It usually occurs between drugs having the same mechanism.
that the combined effect of two drugs is greater than the sum of their individual effects (1+1=3).
The two drugs usually have different mechanisms of action.
Similar to synergism but in potentiation, the effect of one drug itself is greatly increased by intake of another drug that has no effect (i.e. 1+0=2),
